19771-henrietta-temple-a-love-story:
Benjamin Disraeli wrote Henrietta Temple as a love story, published in 1837. Its background reaches back to Tudor risings under Henry the Eighth. A Lord Tewkesbury in the tale was beheaded after a failed rebellion. His estates were forfeited and his blood attainted. A younger branch of the family turned Protestant and married into Walsingham's line. Old disgrace shadows the lovers' world.

Disraeli, later prime minister, began as a fashionable novelist. Henrietta Temple is his most direct love story. It draws on his own early passion, lightly disguised. Politics stays at the edges; feeling takes the center. Readers meet the romantic before the statesman formed. The novel helps explain Disraeli's lifelong taste for drama.
19925-at-the-sign-of-the-barber-s-pole-s:
William Andrews wrote At the Sign of the Barber's Pole as studies in hirsute history. Old shop signs have mostly been swept away, he notes. The pawnbroker's three brass balls survive, and so does the barber's pole. Round those relics Andrews builds his chapters. Beards, shaving, and barbers' customs across centuries fill them. The tone is antiquarian and amused throughout.

Andrews collected curious history by profession and delight. Hair makes a surprisingly rich thread through social life. Kings, priests, and soldiers all legislated the chin. The barber was once surgeon as well as shaver. Andrews records that double trade in detail. His book is a small classic of trade folklore.
20105-the-land-we-live-in-the-story-of-o:
Henry Mann published The Land We Live In in 1896, the story of the United States told for general readers. For the Battle of New Orleans, Mann draws on a rare source. Vincent Nolte wrote Fifty Years in Both Hemispheres, printed in Hamburg in 1853. Nolte owned the cotton that Jackson seized before that battle.

Nolte also served as a volunteer in the fight itself. Mann treats him as a strong voice on what truly happened there. The book moves through the nation's growth in a clear, brisk line. Readers get American history with an eye for firsthand tales and odd details.
20258-hunter-s-marjory:
Hunter's Marjory is a story for girls, set in woods and country homes. Marjory's dog begins to whine softly as her own mood shifts. Suddenly the whines turn to growls deep in his throat. He shakes free of her arms and stares into the wood beyond.

A dog's alarm in such tales often warns of danger close at hand. Marjory must face whatever waits among the trees with nerve. Girls' stories of the era prize courage, kindness, and quick thought. Readers get a wholesome tale where a girl and her dog stand together.
20297-ten-american-girls-from-history:
Kate Dickinson Sweetser published Ten American Girls from History in 1917. One tale opens with warriors marching in single file through forest settlements. They lead a captive white man to Powhatan for judgment and sentence. Crowds of onlookers hurry in along the wood trails to see him.

That captive is Captain John Smith, in the famed Pocahontas story. Sweetser retells such moments through the eyes of ten real girls. Each girl stands at a turning point in early American history. Young readers get biography, adventure, and patriotism in short, vivid lives.
20357-jerry:
Jean Webster published Jerry in 1907, a light novel of Americans in Italy. Jerry jokes that a letter is indeed a love-letter, since Gustavo asks. In fact, his sister writes that they arrive tonight by train. They will pull out for Riva by the first boat tomorrow.

Lake Garda's Riva gives the tale its sunny Italian stage. Webster, famed for Daddy-Long-Legs, writes with wit and warm economy. Jerry's banter hides a growing love he teases others about freely. Readers get a bright, brief romance in Webster's clear, charming style.
20384-david-lannarck-midget-an-adventure:
David Lannarck, Midget is an adventure story about a circus performer of very small stature. David leaves the show world behind him. He becomes friends with big, rangy Sam Welborn, and the circus midget decides to make his home in the wide open spaces of the West.

The friendship between the tiny performer and the big ranchman drives the tale. David must prove himself in a land built for larger men. The story mixes humour, loyalty, and outdoor adventure, and it gives young readers a hero who wins by grit and good sense rather than size.
20436-sunshine-factory:
Pansy, the pen name of Isabella Alden, wrote Sunshine Factory as a story for children about making cheer at home. Its young characters learn to bring light into dull days. A kind grown-up, Uncle Jack, shows them how play can be made from almost nothing.

Uncle Jack teaches a girl to cut holes in paper for a mask. He shows her how to cut a whole family of paper dolls, and pretty things for Willie. Then he takes a tea tray and rolls a marble round it. The book's lessons ride on such small, warm scenes.
20516-christmas-a-story:
Zona Gale's Christmas: A Story is set in Old Trail Town, the small town she made famous in her fiction. The town watches a quiet wonder in one woman's garden. There she has a great patch of purple violets blooming out of season.

All Old Trail Town takes account of its neighbors' flowers, of the migratory birds, and of eclipses. So the whole town comes to see the wonder of violets at Christmas. Gale builds her tale of giving around that bloom, in the plain, tender style that won her a wide and loyal readership.
20548-the-secret-of-the-storm-country:
Grace Miller White's The Secret of the Storm Country, published in 1916, continues the story she began in Tess of the Storm Country. The scene is the squatter country along Cayuga Lake in New York. It opens in the lazy warmth of a May afternoon.

That spring follows Orn Skinner's release from Auburn Prison. Three men lounge on the shore in front of Satisfied Longman's shack, with the lake waters at their feet. Old wrongs and a hidden secret hang over the settlement. White's tale mixes romance and hardship among the fisher folk of the lake.
20584-you-should-worry-says-john-henry:
George V. Hobart's You Should Worry, Says John Henry, published in 1914, collects the slang monologues of his comic hero John Henry. John Henry is a cheerful New York sport with an opinion on everything. Dance crazes, schemes, and city types all pass through his talk.

We are not a couple of patsies with the pumps, he protests. We can learn enough in two lessons to make good in this boob community. He vows to start a tango craze that will put life and ginger in the whole outfit. Hobart's John Henry books caught the street slang of their decade exactly.
20620-rosemary:
Rosemary is a novel for girls about three sisters in a quiet house, watched closely in the opening scene. Sunlight picks out their hair one by one. One head glows a deep red, and another turns to a fairy web of spun yellow silk. The light searches out a faint copper tint in the dark locks of the third.

The girls sit motionless, their faces turned toward the stairs, as silent as everything else in that silent house. From that held breath, the story opens into the sisters' home life, work, and hopes. Rosemary herself carries the book's warmth, in the domestic series fiction of its day.
20756-rabbi-and-priest-a-story:
Milton Goldsmith published Rabbi and Priest in 1891, a tale of Russian Jewish life. The preface owns that names and dates are not strictly exact. Still, it follows Mendel Winenki from boyhood to old age with care.

Through Mendel, readers see the faith, pain, and pride of a scorned people. A rabbi and a priest stand for two worlds that clash and meet. Goldsmith aimed to win fair thought for Russian Jews in hard times. The book mixes story with plea, a common shape for fiction that hoped to soften real hate in its readers.
20782-triplanetary:
Two patrol ships vanish without a word in Triplanetary, and a captain draws the grim lesson. At three losses, he says, it would get to be a habit. Detector screens and new arms guard his own ship, yet clear ether feels like a trap.

E. E. Smith opens his Lensman saga with space war on a vast scale. Alien foes, bold fleets, and secret plans span ages of hidden strife. Smith's tales set the mold for grand space opera in the pulp age. Readers who like vast stakes and swift action will find this first book a brisk start.
20805-lloyd-george-the-man-and-his-story:
A Welsh countryside boy found no path up, so he moved to Manchester to teach. There his son David was born on January 17, 1863. That boy, Lloyd George, would rise to lead Britain in war and peace.

The Man and His Story, from 1917, traces that climb while it still unfolded. Village roots, law, Parliament, and reform mark the stages of the tale. Lloyd George pushed pensions, insurance, and bold budgets before the war. When this life came out, he had just taken the top post. Readers get a wartime portrait of a leader at his peak.
20848-an-elementary-study-of-chemistry:
A full list of the elements waits in the appendix of An Elementary Study of Chemistry. Stars mark the common ones a pupil must know well. A third of the whole list, the book says, suffices for sound basic grasp.

William McPherson and William Henderson built this text for first courses in the science. Atoms, gases, metals, and acids proceed in clear, tested order. Lab work and plain talk share the pages. The book shows how American colleges taught chemistry then. It stays firm on facts and keen on experiment throughout.
20912-the-daffodil-mystery:
Thornton Lyne lounges at his desk, too sure of his own genius to heed a warning look. Edgar Wallace opens The Daffodil Mystery on that sober grey-eyed gaze. Lyne's wealth and pride set him square in a killer's path.

Wallace, king of the fast thriller, spins murder, blackmail, and London low life here. Daffodils left with the dead give the case its odd name. Short chapters and sharp twists keep the pages turning at speed. The book shows why Wallace ruled crime fiction in his day: no fuss, no pause, just plot wound tight as wire.
20967-a-guide-to-peterborough-cathedral-:
Peada, son of Penda of Mercia, founded the monastery of Medeshamstede in 655, this guide recounts. The Saxon chronicler counts 5,850 winters from the world's birth to that reign. A Guide to Peterborough Cathedral opens its brief history at that deep root.

From Saxon minster to Norman giant, the cathedral's growth fills the guide's pages. Tombs, chapels, carved bosses, and buried queens mark the guided walk. Katharine of Aragon and Mary, Queen of Scots both once lay here. Small guides like this taught Victorian visitors to read a great church stone by stone, saint by saint.
20992-tom-dick-and-harry:
Cold sweat, shaking limbs, and hair on end wake the teller of Tom, Dick and Harry. He sits bolt upright at midnight, chin on knees, in a grip of fright. Talbot Baines Reed opens his school tale on that raw, comic scare.

Three boys whose names became a phrase for any lads at all star here. Reed's school world of dorms, games, and scrapes fills the tale with life. He wrote scores of such tales for The Boy's Own Paper and kin. This one shows his warm, brisk touch, with fear and fun in near equal parts from the first dark page.
20996-an-epoch-in-history:
Four hundred ninety-nine trained teachers sailed from San Francisco to school a new land. P. H. Eley calls that sailing An Epoch in History in his 1904 book. Their task: plant free public schools through the whole Philippine Islands.

The Thomasites, as those teachers were named, reached Manila in 1901 aboard the Thomas. Eley, himself of that band, tells of schools raised from bare rooms. Language, custom, and war's wreckage made the work vast and slow. His book keeps a proud, dated view of America's school crusade in its new Pacific colony.
21070-a-middy-of-the-slave-squadron-a-we:
One of the last books Harry Collingwood wrote, this West African story puts a young midshipman aboard His Majesty's corvette Psyche. First Lieutenant Perry mops his brow in the heat as the ship works against the slave trade. The squadron patrolled the coast to intercept slave ships.

Collingwood was a naval architect in real life, and his handling of sea terms is exact throughout. Orders, skylights, and night watches are rendered by a man who knew ships from the drawing board. The tale gives young readers patrol duty, danger, and discipline on the West African station, told in his late, practised style.
21095-she-and-i-volume-1-a-love-story-a-:
John Conroy Hutcheson is known for sea stories. But this early novel stays in a dull London suburb just after the middle of the nineteenth century. Its hero spots a pretty young woman in church and falls in love at once. His first problem is simply getting an introduction.

He manages that, but the girl's mother looks hard at money: the hero is not well off, while richer suitors are less likeable. Church parties and outings move the courtship along until the wooing seems to succeed. Hutcheson fills chapters with poems and foreign quotes, in a style quite unlike his later nautical books.
21096-she-and-i-volume-2-a-love-story-a-:
Volume Two of John Conroy Hutcheson's love story keeps the same cast as the first. The vicar and Miss Pimpernell, Lady Dasher and her daughters, curate Mawley, and Min Clyde all return. The hero, Lorton, loves Min, the girl with the striking grey eyes. Their affair now deepens toward its outcome.

Hutcheson opens with a dream of Min and quotes Shakespeare on dreams before plunging back into visits, doubts, and jealousy. French, German, Italian, Latin, and even Greek quotes dot the pages, as in Volume One. The two volumes together form a full Victorian courtship, told as a life history.
21102-tom-and-some-other-girls-a-public-:
Rhoda Chester has been taught at home by governesses while her brothers went out into the world. When her German governess leaves to marry, her father decides Rhoda should try boarding school at last. Her mother dislikes the idea, but Rhoda herself is keen to go.

Mrs George de Horne Vaizey sends Rhoda among Tom and the other girls of the title, where she enjoys school and does well. Then an important exam looms, and Rhoda overworks until her brain fails her in the exam hall. The story treats ambition, health, and friendship among schoolgirls of the period with unusual sympathy.
21107-on-board-the-esmeralda-martin-leig:
Martin Leigh loses his naval officer father in Africa and then his mother. He is left to an uncle's household, where Aunt Matilda makes his life miserable. John Conroy Hutcheson sends the orphan to a cheap boarding school whose fine prospectus hides grim reality. Martin bears it for years, helped by his friend Tom.

After a Guy Fawkes prank brings expulsion, the boys run away and stow aboard a small coaster. Its captain beats them worse than their headmaster had. Martin's log then follows him to kindness, to sea aboard the Esmeralda, through fire and wreck off South America, and home again.
21118-etheldreda-the-ready-a-school-stor:
The Saxon family's Christmas holidays start with parties and pleasure in Mrs George de Horne Vaizey's school story, then a shadow falls without warning. Mr Saxon hides in his study looking old and worn. Mrs Saxon smiles a twisted smile and sends for the governess, Miss Bruce, in haste.

The parents slip away to their country house on some worrying errand, leaving the household in suspense. Etheldreda, the ready and capable girl of the title, stands at the centre of the family as trouble unfolds. Vaizey mixes schoolgirl life with a household mystery, keeping the tone warm even when the parents' secret hangs over everything.
21123-english-literature-and-society-in-:
Leslie Stephen delivered these Ford Lectures at Oxford in 1903, though illness kept him from reading them himself. His nephew Herbert Fisher read them aloud in his place, and Stephen published them in London in 1904. The lectures ask how social conditions shaped English writing in the eighteenth century.

Stephen argues that literature grows from the life of its age: its readers, publishers, coffee houses, and class habits. The book is divided into five chapters from the six lecture sections. Written in Stephen's clear, dry style, it became a lasting short study of the age of Pope, Johnson, and the rising reading public.
21210-thomas-davis-selections-from-his-p:
Thomas Davis, the young poet of Ireland's Nation newspaper, died at thirty in 1845, and this selection gathers his prose and poetry in one volume. T. W. Rolleston introduces the book for the Library of Irish Literature series. It opens with Davis's study defending the Irish Parliament of James II.

Articles from The Nation and other papers follow, on history, literature, and politics, then a selection of the poems and ballads. Rolleston aimed to give everything of lasting value Davis wrote in prose, plus his best verse. Davis helped invent a cultural nationalism for Ireland, and this volume shows both the arguments and the songs that carried it.
21233-all-s-well-or-alice-s-victory:
Emily Sarah Holt set this novel in the Weald of Kent in 1556, in the first heat of the Reformation. A local family has turned Protestant in private while still seeming Catholic in public. Their priest hears confessions, learns their secret, and carries it to the Bishop.

One young woman of the family, Alice, is strongest in the new faith. She is taken before the Bishop, jailed on straw with only bread and water, and badly treated. Her prison is improved only because she is to be burned alive. Holt wrote many such tales of Protestant sufferers, and Alice's victory is one of faith under sentence of death.
21254-in-africa-hunting-adventures-in-th:
John T. McCutcheon, cartoonist of the Chicago Tribune, traded his drawing board for a rifle. He took an African hunting trip and published this account in 1910. He calls it merely the record of a delightful trip along the Equator. There the roar of the lion and the crack of the rifle still ruled. His own photographs and cartoons illustrate it.

McCutcheon had wanted since boyhood to hunt lions and elephants, unsure whether he would rather be an Indian fighter. In Africa he lives in what he calls a story-book atmosphere of thrilling adventures. The book is dedicated to adventurous souls who resent the beaten path.
21264-the-four-pools-mystery:
Jean Webster, who later wrote Daddy-Long-Legs, published this mystery with the Century Company in 1908. The narrator arrives at Four-Pools Plantation in Virginia, where a ha'nt is said to walk and a robbery stays unsolved. Terry Patten, a New York newspaper man, is on the story's track from the first chapter.

Cat-Eye Mose creates sensations, a detective is sent for and sent back, and an inquest follows a tragedy in a cave near Luray. False clues pile up before Terry searches the abandoned cabins and finds the bonds. Polly's confession and proposal close a mystery mixed with romance and Virginia local colour.
21411-holborn-and-bloomsbury:
Holborn and Bloomsbury, by Sir Walter Besant and G. E. Mitton, forms one part of the Fascination of London set. The booklet came out in 1903, after Besant's death, from his great survey of the city. Its aim was to save the history held in London's streets.

The authors walk two districts rich in old inns, courts, and homes of writers. Staple Inn, at Holborn Bars, stands at the front as a famed survivor. Street by street, the book ties places to the folk who lived and worked there. Local readers and students of London both find much to keep here.
21431-mary-powell-deborah-s-diary:
Anne Manning joins two linked tales in Mary Powell and Deborah's Diary, reissued by Dent in 1908. Mary Powell was the wife of John Milton, and her home at Forest Hill still drew visits long after. The last scraps of the house were pulled down in 1854.

Manning tells of Milton's spring, the walnut trees, and the church on the hill near Mary's home. The tales wear the dress and speech of the seventeenth century with care. A warm portrait of Mary, drawn from an old praise of a fair milkmaid, opens the book. It suits readers who love quiet, well-kept historical tales.
21465-hurricane-hurry:
Hurricane Hurry is a long historical novel by W. H. G. Kingston, set around the year 1780. The printed book ran to some four hundred and seventy pages of small type. Its hero bears the odd name Hurry, though the text twice slips and calls him Poynder.

Kingston writes ship and storm with his usual fine touch. By the ninth chapter Hurry has fallen for a young American lady. Her father is a colonel serving on the Rebel side in the war. Love and war thus pull the hero in two ways at once. Sea fights, divided loyalties, and family secrets fill the tale.
21623-usury:
Calvin Elliott attacks interest on money in Usury, a scriptural, ethical, and economic view, copyrighted in 1902. The Anti-Usury League of Millersburg, Ohio, published the book. Elliott begs readers to follow his argument in its set order, as it grew in his own mind.

Chapters move from a definition of usury to the law of Moses. David and Solomon, Jeremiah and Ezekiel, and Nehemiah's reform come in turn. The teachings of the Master and the parables of the talents and pounds get close reading. Elliott builds a full biblical case against lending at interest, step by step.
21649-a-cluster-of-grapes-a-book-of-twen:
Galloway Kyle gathers new verse in A Cluster of Grapes, a book of twentieth-century poetry issued in 1914. His title comes from Sidney's praise of poetry, a cluster given at a vineyard's gate. Kyle refuses to sort his poets into schools or isms.

No group, he insists, is set above another in the gathering. The aim is a taste that makes the reader long to pass further. Poems stand as examples of the present century's art, each under its own author's rights. The slim book serves as a period tasting of British verse on the edge of the Great War.
21663-aunt-mary:
Mrs Perring, who wrote The Story of a Mouse, tells a children's tale in Aunt Mary, issued in 1881. A pretty suburban villa opens the tale, with new neighbours to judge. Mr Maitland and his two sweet children promise pleasant society for the street.

Routledge of London and New York published the book, with a picture of Aunt Mary at the front. Perring's tales of cats, castles, and cottages had already won young readers. Kindness, home manners, and small trials shape the story's world. The book is a fair sample of the gentle, moral tale Victorian children were given to read at home.
21685-the-cockatoo-s-story:
Mrs George Cupples lets a white cockatoo tell his own tale in The Cockatoo's Story, issued in 1881. The bird owns he is ashamed of himself and brought his troubles on his own head. Twelve pictures, from a greedy dog onward, fill the book.

Mrs Polly, a small gray parrot across the room, walks her perch fast and ruffles her feathers. She calls the cockatoo sulky and ungrateful, and offers to peck him well. The boy who owns them, she insists, means only kindness. Chat between caged birds carries a gentle lesson for young readers, in Cupples's known style.
21687-the-youngest-girl-in-the-fifth-a-s:
Angela Brazil promotes Gwen in The Youngest Girl in the Fifth, a school story drawn by Stanley Davis. Gwen protests she has done nothing, under looks fit for a criminal and a martyr. Miss Roscoe's word has moved her up a form, youngest in the Fifth.

Chapters promise a false step, trouble in the Fifth, and a casting vote. Gwen keeps Christmas, turns henwife, meets a storm, and learns first aid. A gymkhana, a tennis tournament, and the Senior Oxford exams crown the year. Gwen to the rescue is the last chapter's promise, in Brazil's bright, loyal school world.
21748-black-ivory:
Black ivory was the traders' grim name for enslaved people, and this Ballantyne novel confronts the East African slave trade head-on. A wreck casts two heroes ashore on the east coast of Africa. There, Arab and Portuguese traders still run their trade despite British patrol ships. The castaways meet a slaver almost where they land.

Rescued by a warship that takes a slaver's dhow, they reach Zanzibar and push inland with fresh funds. What they find in the interior fills most of the book. Ballantyne meant the tale to open young eyes to a trade still alive in his day. It is one of his most earnest books, adventure carrying a real charge of outrage.
21751-the-middy-and-the-moors-an-algerin:
Piracy and slavery on the North African coast drive this Algerine tale by R. M. Ballantyne. A middy, a young naval officer in training, falls into the hands of Moorish captors in the world of Algiers. Ballantyne researched Algiers and deep-sea diving for the book, as the notes to this edition record. The Barbary coast was famed in his day for corsairs and Christian captives.

The tale follows the young sailor through capture, hardship, and the strange life of the city that holds him. Escape and rescue hang over every chapter. Ballantyne writes it as a boy's adventure with a serious core. It asks what slavery meant in a foreign land, and what courage freedom took.
21891-the-brand-of-silence-a-detective-s:
Fog in New York harbor opens The Brand of Silence, a 1919 detective story by Harrington Strong, issued by Street and Smith's Chelsea House. The tramp steamer Manatee wallows in from a three-day fight with the ocean, rusty and lurching like a drunk. Aboard her come a girl, some discourtesies, and the first threads of the mystery. A man called Murk stands near the center of it.

Chapters promise battered keys, liars, a moment of violence, and a startling story before the truth comes out. Strong writes in the pulp manner: short chapters, sharp turns, and a campaign planned like a battle. Kate Gilbert's part and a trip up the river deepen the plot. It is a brisk period mystery, built to be read at one sitting.
21913-the-talking-leaves-an-indian-story:
Two girls on a mountain watch a crowd of men stoop and hunt in the grass in William O. Stoddard's The Talking Leaves, an Indian story of 1882. Rita leans over her pony's neck, her long hair falling, while Ni-ha-be sits still in her silver-mounted saddle. The air is so clear among the snow-capped ranges that far things seem close. The men below have found something in the grass, and hunt for more.

Talking leaves is the girls' world name for written pages, and paper drives the mystery. Stoddard wrote many tales of the frontier for young readers. His West mixes scouts, native peoples, and lost parties in bright mountain light. The two heroines, alike in size and unlike in all else, carry the tale's wonder.
21944-the-pleasant-street-partnership-a-:
A shop run as a neighborhood partnership anchors Mary F. Leonard's The Pleasant Street Partnership, a story published in 1903. The Terrace where the tale sits is rather far downtown, with the busy city closing in on commonplace houses, schools, and noisy car lines. A wave of improvement starts the chapters. Chapters follow the naming of the shop, an alien arrival, and Miss Wilbur's place in the scheme.

Leonard writes of loyalty, spools of twist, and the adventures of a birthday cake with a neighbor's eye. Charlotte, to whom the book is offered, presides over its affections. Frank T. Merrill drew the small boy surveying the partners with great composure. It is a cozy American neighborhood story, where trade and friendship share one counter.
21953-aurelian-or-rome-in-the-third-cent:
Rome under the Emperor Aurelian is rebuilt in letters in William Ware's Aurelian, a historical novel first issued in 1838. The tale is told as letters of Lucius M. Piso from Rome to Fausta, daughter of Gracchus, at Palmyra. It follows Ware's Zenobia, and was first named Probus before foreign editions settled on the better title. This fifth edition of 1874 gathers both volumes in one.

Zenobia's Palmyra and Aurelian's campaigns stand behind the letters. Ware, a Unitarian minister, loved the early Church's world and stocked his fiction with its debates. Pagan Rome and rising Christianity meet in his pages. The novel was among the earliest American works of Roman historical fiction, and readers abroad reprinted it for decades.
21964-the-short-story:
Nine master tales teach the short story form in this 1916 school anthology edited by W. Patterson Atkinson of Lincoln High School, Jersey City. Atkinson opens with a history: mankind has always loved tales, from the storyteller at the cave mouth onward. His contents run from Irving's Rip Van Winkle through Poe's Gold Bug and Purloined Letter to Hawthorne's Birthmark. Bret Harte's Outcasts of Poker Flat and Stevenson's Markheim follow.

Kipling's Wee Willie Winkie closes the set, with notes and a bibliography behind it. Portraits of the authors face their tales. Atkinson defines the form, traces its growth, and sorts its kinds before letting the masters speak. Generations of American schoolchildren met the short story here first, in a book built to be taught from and loved.
21969-the-outcry:
Old pictures in a great house stir modern greed in Henry James's last completed novel, The Outcry, published in 1911. Banks the servant reports that no stranger has yet arrived at Dedborough Place. Lady Sandgate crosses the hall, a folded telegram pink in her hand, to meet Lord John. Around them the house breathes two hushed centuries of stored treasure: portraits, cabinets, and tapestries of high distinction.

The outcry of the title is the public noise raised when national treasures are sold to foreign buyers. James turns an art sale into a comedy of manners and morals. Love and money tug at the same canvas. Written first as a play, the novel moves in scenes of brilliant talk. It is late James at his most theatrical.
22002-a-simple-story:
Elizabeth Inchbald wrote A Simple Story, first printed in 1791 and reprinted many times after. Inchbald had spent thirteen years on the stage despite a speech impediment. In her preface she admits the book was written through weariness, not inspiration. The story centres on Miss Milner, a lively young ward, and her grave guardian Dorriforth.

Miss Milner falls in love with the man meant to guide and correct her. Pride, temper, and rash acts wreck what might have been a happy match. Years later the tale turns to her daughter, who must face a cold house and a bitter father. Readers still value the book for its sharp scenes and its honest picture of feeling ruled by pride.
22057-kid-wolf-of-texas-a-western-story:
Ward M. Stevens published Kid Wolf of Texas, a western story, in 1930. His hero rides into view whistling a Texas tune. Kid Wolf is a lean young rider in fringed buckskin touched with bright Southwest colours. His California stock saddle is decorated with silver conchas, and he sits his horse like part of the animal.

Stevens wrote for the cheap western trade, where a hero's look told readers what to expect. Fast riding, gunplay, and a code of honour drive such tales. Kid Wolf's adventures belong to the pulp years, when westerns filled newsstands every week. The book is a plain sample of that hard-riding popular fiction.
22064-tess-of-the-storm-country:
Grace Miller White published Tess of the Storm Country in 1909, and it became her best-known novel. Tessibel Skinner is a squatter's daughter living by Cayuga Lake near Ithaca. The squatter law let her people keep land once they raised a hut on it. But the authorities kept tightening the game laws until the fishermen dared only draw their nets by night, though the fish were their food.

Tess fights for her father, her baby charge, and her people's right to live. A rich man's son and a young minister cross her rough world. White's melodrama was filmed again and again, once with Mary Pickford. It still defines the storm-country squatters for most readers.
22173-the-grell-mystery:
Frank Froest, a former Scotland Yard superintendent, wrote The Grell Mystery in 1913. Froest knew police work from the inside, and his fiction shows it. Robert Grell, the victim at the story's centre, was a daring explorer famous on two continents. His friend Fairfield, a writer on travel and peoples, matches him in fame.

Grell's murder sets detectives hunting through London clubs and beyond. Froest builds his case from clues, timetables, and patient inquiry rather than genius flashes. The book appeared just before the Great War, in detective fiction's golden dawn. It remains a solid specimen of the police novel written by a real policeman.
22179-old-rail-fence-corners-the-a-b-c-s:
Old Rail Fence Corners calls itself the A.B.C.'s of Minnesota history. Lucy Leavenworth Wilder Morris started the project, gathering tales from the state's old settlers. the-french-revolution-a-history: Thomas Carlyle's 1837 thundering history of the French Revolution, written in a prophetic, biblical style all his own. The storming of the Bastille, the Terror, and Napoleon rise like a great drama. Exhausting and exhilarating, it is history as epic poetry and one of the Victorian age's defining books.
the-golf-course-mystery: A detective novel by Chester K. Steele about a murder on the links and the investigator who solves it. Fair-play puzzling in the classic mode, with golf-course atmosphere. Light, clever Golden Age entertainment.
the-green-mirror-a-quiet-story: The Green Mirror, a quiet story by Hugh Walpole. The mirror's tale. This book preserves that novel. It waits for future eyes. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
the-law-of-the-land-of-miss-lady-whom-it: Emerson Hough, chronicler of the American West, sets this novel on the frontier where law was still being made. Miss Lady and John Eddring are drawn into mystery and danger in a land settling its accounts. Hough's deep knowledge of western history gives the romance and adventure an authentic ring.
the-library: Andrew Lang's The Library: essays on books, collecting, and the love of reading. Bibliophilic and charming, it is the classic of book love. For everyone who cherishes books. Lang on books is pure pleasure, pure pleasure for book lovers.
the-life-of-william-carey-shoemaker-miss: George Smith tells the story of William Carey, the poor shoemaker who sailed to India and became the father of modern missions. Bible translation, schools, and stubborn faith fill this inspiring life. A classic of missionary biography.
the-love-of-books-the-philobiblon-of-ric: Written in 1345 by Richard de Bury, bishop and book-collector, the Philobiblon is the first great love letter to books in English literature. In elegant Latin prose he praises learning, scolds book-destroyers, and gives practical advice on collecting and caring for manuscripts. Medieval in origin but timeless in feeling, it speaks directly to every reader who has ever loved a library.
the-mahatma-and-the-hare-a-dream-story: H. Rider Haggard's dream story of the mahatma and the hare: a plea for animals. Mystical and moving, it shows his spiritual side. A curious Haggard, haggard dreams of kindness to beasts, a strange and moving plea.
the-mill-mystery: Anna Katharine Green — called the mother of the American detective novel — spins a classic whodunit around a body found at a lonely mill. Her gentleman detective Ebenezer Gryce follows clues and red herrings with Victorian thoroughness. Published in 1886, the book helped invent the rules of mystery fiction that writers still follow.
the-monastery: Walter Scott sets this historical novel in the Scottish Borders during the Reformation, when old Catholic monasteries faced a new Protestant order. The monks of Melrose watch their world crumble while young heroes navigate love and loyalty amid religious upheaval. Rich in Scots character and historical color, it is Scott doing what he did best — bringing a vanished age to life.
the-poorhouse-waif-and-his-divine-teache: Isabel Byrum tells the true story of a poorhouse waif found by his divine Teacher — a tale of rescue, faith, and a changed life. Written to touch hearts and win souls. A moving little book of Christian witness. From the poorhouse to a life of faith, his story shows the power of grace to remake a life.
the-red-house-mystery: A. A. Milne's 1922 detective novel, the only mystery by the creator of Winnie-the-Pooh. A murder at the Red House, an amateur sleuth, and fair-play puzzling in the classic style. Charming, clever, and very English.
the-renaissance-studies-in-art-and-poetr: Walter Pater's 1873 book found the Renaissance in Botticelli's spring and Leonardo's smile. His call to burn with a hard flame made art a creed. Exquisite, daring, and hugely influential: the bible of the beautiful. Pater's Mona Lisa still smiles from these pages.
the-rosary: Florence Barclay's The Rosary is a beloved Edwardian romance. A plain, good-hearted woman wins a handsome man's heart through sheer goodness. The tender story melted the hearts of millions of readers. Love's quiet triumph, simply and sweetly told.
the-secret-adversary: Agatha Christie's 1922 thriller introducing Tommy and Tuppence, her young adventurers-for-hire. Hunting a missing treaty and a vanished girl through postwar London, the bright young things stumble into a real conspiracy. Lively, romantic, and fun, it launched Christie's second great detective team.
the-sheridan-road-mystery: The Sheridan Road Mystery is a detective story set in old Chicago. A puzzling and daring crime baffles the police along the lake. The keen sleuth follows clue after clue to the truth. A brisk and satisfying American mystery.
the-wreck-of-the-golden-mary: A Christmas story by Dickens and Wilkie Collins about the wreck of the Golden Mary and her crew's fight to live. Told in turn by the survivors, it blends high-seas adventure with Dickens's warm humanity. First published in 1856, it is gripping Victorian disaster fiction with a holiday frame.
the-young-enchanted-a-romantic-story: The Young Enchanted, a romantic story by Hugh Walpole. The enchanted youth. This book preserves that novel. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
torquemada-and-the-spanish-inquisition-a: Torquemada and the Spanish Inquisition, Rafael Sabatini's history of the Grand Inquisitor. The dark tribunal's tale. This book preserves that history. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
tudela-itinerary:
Benjamin of Tudela, a Jewish traveler from Navarre, journeyed across the known world in the years around 1160. His Itinerary, in Marcus Adler's translation, reports what he found from Spain to Baghdad and beyond. It is the medieval world's most important travel narrative of its kind.

Benjamin counts Jewish communities in city after city, noting their scholars, trades, and numbers. He also describes Rome, Constantinople, Jerusalem, and Baghdad with a merchant's eye for wealth and power. Tales of distant lands, some fabulous, close the route home. Historians mine the book for facts found nowhere else. Adler's notes trace his route and test his claims against other sources.
umbrellas-and-their-history: William Sangster tells the odd, gay story of the umbrella — from old Eastern sunshades to the staid Victorian standby. Makers, modes, and merry tales crowd a book that proves no theme too slight for good telling. Daily things, it seems, have the best pasts.
unconscious-memory: Samuel Butler — the iconoclastic author of Erewhon — argues in this provocative book that heredity is a form of memory passed unconsciously from parent to child. Written against Darwin's followers, it proposes that instinct is inherited habit. Controversial in its day and still fascinating, it shows one of Victorian England's most original minds at full tilt.
washington-up-from-slavery:
Booker Washington published Up from Slavery in 1901, and it became the most influential Black memoir of its era. Born enslaved in Virginia, Washington taught himself to read after emancipation. At twenty-five he founded the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama.

He tells of working in salt furnaces and coal mines to reach Hampton Institute. At Tuskegee he built a school from almost nothing, brick by brick, with student labor. His Atlanta speech of 1895, urging work and patience, made him a national figure. Critics then and since have debated his bargain with segregation, but the book's reach is beyond doubt.
wild-wales-its-people-language-and-scene: George Borrow's 1862 travel memoir of walking through Wales, talking with everyone he met. Passionate about languages, Borrow records Welsh speech, songs, and legends while sketching vivid portraits of innkeepers, preachers, and mountain folk. Part travelogue and part love letter to a culture, it is one of the most personal books of the Victorian age.
zuleika-dobson-or-an-oxford-love-story: Max Beerbohm's 1911 comic masterpiece: the beautiful Zuleika visits Oxford, and every undergraduate falls in love and drowns himself. Witty, exquisite, and utterly absurd, it is the great Oxford novel. Perfection in comedy. Beerbohm's only novel is a flawless comedy of vanity and doom.
